theory.md: A firm is worth all the money it will give in the future. But €1 later is worth less than €1 today. So we pull every future cash flow back to today (we **discount** it) and add them up. That sum is the value of the **whole firm**. The firm belongs to lenders and owners: take away what belongs to the lenders (debt) and the rest belongs to the owners (equity).
A lemonade stand pays you €10 every year, forever. You could earn 10% elsewhere. Value today = 10 / 0.10 = **€100**. If it grows 2% a year: 10 / (0.10 − 0.02) = **€125**.

theory.caption: Every arrow = divide by \((1+\text{WACC})^t\). The terminal value sits at t = 3, so it is discounted 3 times, not 4.

theory.title: The 6-step recipe (always the same)
items: **Write the formulas first.** Old solutions give points for stating them.
**Cash flows for years 1–3.** Start with year 1, not year 0. With \(CF_0\) and growth \(g\): \(CF_1=CF_0\cdot(1+g)\), \(CF_2=CF_1\cdot(1+g)\), …
**Terminal value at t = 3:** \(TV_3=\frac{CF_4}{\text{WACC}-g}\) with \(CF_4=CF_3\cdot(1+g)\). No growth: \(TV_3=\frac{CF}{\text{WACC}}\).
**Discount** every CF and the TV with \((1+\text{WACC})^t\) and add them up = firm value. Add non-operating assets if given.
**Equity = firm value − MARKET value of debt** (never the book value).
**Compare and decide:** equity value vs market cap (or value per share vs share price). Higher → undervalued → **buy**. Lower → overvalued → **sell**.

theory.md: Market cap 80m, 12m shares, book debt 45m, **market debt 50m**, CF 10m for 3 years, then 11m growing 1%, WACC 8%.

theory.title: Variants that appeared in old exams
theory.md:
- **Growth from \(CF_0\):** \(CF_0=300\)m, +1% for 3 years, then +0.5% → \(CF_1=303\), \(CF_4=310.64\), \(TV_3=5{,}647.9\) → equity 4,559.8m → 45.60 € per share → buy at 40.
- **Flat CF, then a new flat level:** 6m for 3 years, then 6.5m forever, WACC 7% → \(TV_3=\frac{6.5}{0.07}=92.86\) → equity 59.55m > 50m → buy.
- **Revenue multiple:** "peer firm value = 3.5 × sales" → our firm value \(=3.5\times24\text{m}=84\text{m}\). Just multiply.

standardAnswer.md:
Since we value the firm with the ==entity method==, we discount the ==free cash flows to the firm== with the ==WACC== of 8%. The ==terminal value== at the end of year 3 is \(TV_3=\frac{CF_4}{\text{WACC}-g}=\frac{11}{0.08-0.01}=157.14\text{m}\), discounted to today 124.75m.

\(\text{Firm value}=9.26+8.57+7.94+124.75=150.52\text{m}\). The ==value of equity== is the firm value minus the ==market value of debt==: \(150.52-50=100.52\text{m}\).

The ==intrinsic value== of equity (100.52m, 8.38 € per share) is higher than the ==market capitalisation== (80m, 6.67 € per share). The share is ==undervalued==, so I recommend to ==buy==.

tasks.name: DCF → equity value → buy or sell

variants.text:
Market capitalisation 80m, 12m shares outstanding. Book value of debt 45m, **market value of debt 50m**. Free cash flows: 10m in each of the next 3 years, then 11m growing at 1% forever. WACC 8%.

Calculate the firm value, the equity value and the value per share. Should you buy or sell the share?

solution.md: Subtract the **market** value of debt (50m), never the book value (45m).

tasks.name: Explain the entity method
tasks.question: Explain how a firm is valued with the **entity method** (DCF) and how you get from the firm value to a buy or sell recommendation.

checklist.text: Discount **free cash flows to the firm** with the **WACC**
Explicit forecast period plus a **terminal value** \(TV=\frac{CF_{T+1}}{\text{WACC}-g}\)
Equity = firm value − **market value** of debt
Compare equity value (or value per share) with market cap (or share price)
Conclusion: higher → **undervalued → buy**, lower → overvalued → sell

modelAnswer.md:
With the ==entity method== we discount the ==free cash flows to the firm== with the ==WACC==. We forecast the cash flows explicitly for a few years and capture everything after that with a ==terminal value==, \(TV_T=\frac{CF_{T+1}}{\text{WACC}-g}\).

The sum of all present values is the ==firm value==. Subtracting the ==market value of debt== gives the ==equity value==. If the equity value (or value per share) is higher than the market capitalisation (or share price), the share is ==undervalued== and I recommend to buy it; otherwise sell.

tasks.name: Quick check: the classic DCF traps

questions.q: Cash flows are given for years 1–3. With how many periods do you discount \(TV_3\)?
questions.explain: \(TV_3\) sits at the end of year 3, so it is discounted with \((1+\text{WACC})^3\). Using 4 is the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which debt value do you subtract from the firm value?
options: Face value of the next bond
questions.explain: Equity is what remains after paying lenders at today's value, so you use the **market** value.
Shares are claims on equity, not on the whole firm.

cards.front: From firm value to equity value
cards.back: Equity = firm value − **market** value of debt (not book value).
Equity value > market cap (or value per share > price) → undervalued → **buy**. Otherwise sell.

cards.front: Entity method: which cash flows, which rate?
cards.back: Free cash flows **to the firm**, discounted with the **WACC**.

mistakes: Discounting the TV with \(1.08^4\) instead of \(1.08^3\).
Dividing the **firm** value by the number of shares (must be equity).
hook: **CF – TV – PV – minus D – compare**: cash flows (from year 1) → terminal value → present values → minus debt (market!) → compare with the price.
